title: Include Empty Departments with LEFT JOIN
description_markdown: Use a LEFT JOIN from `departments` to `employees` so that departments without employees are preserved. Return `d.dept_name` and `e.first_name`. Order by `d.dept_name` ASC, `(e.first_name IS NULL)`, `e.first_name` ASC.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN from departments
SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON ...
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, (e.first_name IS NULL), e.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: LEFT JOIN retains all rows from the left table (`departments`), inserting NULL where no matching row exists in `employees`. MySQL sorts NULLs last using `(col IS NULL)` boolean expression.
alternative_solutions: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC;
common_mistakes: Using NULLS LAST keyword which is not supported in MySQL syntax.
dialect_notes: MySQL does not support NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST; use (col IS NULL) to order nulls last in ASC order.
hints: Use `FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id`.
To sort nulls last in MySQL: `ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, (e.first_name IS NULL), e.first_name ASC`.
Query: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, (e.first_name IS NULL), e.first_name ASC;

title: Customer Order Counts Including Zero Orders
description_markdown: Using a LEFT JOIN from `customers` to `orders`, count how many orders each customer has placed as `total_orders`. Return `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, and `COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders`. Group by `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`. Order by `total_orders` DESC, `c.customer_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN and COUNT(o.order_id)
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY total_orders DESC, c.customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Using `COUNT(o.order_id)` instead of `COUNT(*)` correctly counts 0 for customers with no orders.
hints: Crucial: use `COUNT(o.order_id)` so non-matching rows return 0 instead of 1.
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY total_orders DESC, c.customer_id ASC;

title: Emulate FULL OUTER JOIN via UNION in MySQL
description_markdown: MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN natively. Emulate a FULL OUTER JOIN between `professors` and `courses` on `professor_id` by combining a `LEFT JOIN` and a `RIGHT JOIN` using `UNION`. Return `COALESCE(p.last_name, 'No Professor') AS faculty_member`, and `COALESCE(c.course_name, 'No Course Assigned') AS assigned_course`. Order by `faculty_member` ASC, `assigned_course` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Emulate FULL OUTER JOIN with LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN
SELECT ...
FROM professors p LEFT JOIN courses c ON ...
UNION
SELECT ...
FROM professors p RIGHT JOIN courses c ON ...
solution_query: SELECT COALESCE(p.last_name, 'No Professor') AS faculty_member, COALESCE(c.course_name, 'No Course Assigned') AS assigned_course FROM professors p LEFT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id UNION SELECT COALESCE(p.last_name, 'No Professor') AS faculty_member, COALESCE(c.course_name, 'No Course Assigned') AS assigned_course FROM professors p RIGHT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id ORDER BY faculty_member ASC, assigned_course ASC;
solution_explanation: Because MySQL does not support the FULL OUTER JOIN keyword, combining a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION simulates full outer join behavior.
common_mistakes: Using the FULL OUTER JOIN keyword, which causes a syntax error in MySQL.
dialect_notes: MySQL does not implement FULL OUTER JOIN syntax. The standard idiom is to combine LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN queries using UNION.
hints: Combine two queries with UNION: one using `LEFT JOIN` and one using `RIGHT JOIN`.
In both queries, project `COALESCE(p.last_name, 'No Professor') AS faculty_member` and `COALESCE(c.course_name, 'No Course Assigned') AS assigned_course`.

Query: SELECT COALESCE(p.last_name, 'No Professor') AS faculty_member, COALESCE(c.course_name, 'No Course Assigned') AS assigned_course FROM professors p LEFT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id UNION SELECT COALESCE(p.last_name, 'No Professor') AS faculty_member, COALESCE(c.course_name, 'No Course Assigned') AS assigned_course FROM professors p RIGHT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id ORDER BY faculty_member ASC, assigned_course ASC;

title: Include Inactive Customers with LEFT JOIN
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`. Return `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, and `o.order_id`. Order results by `c.customer_id` ascending, then `o.order_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN customers and orders
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC, o.order_id ASC;
solution_explanation: LEFT JOIN retains every customer record from the left table, displaying NULL for order_id if the customer has placed no orders.
common_mistakes: Using INNER JOIN, which accidentally eliminates customers without purchase history.
interview_tip: When user engagement or churn analysis is needed, LEFT JOIN ensures the denominator includes the full cohort.
hints: Use `FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id`.
Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC, o.order_id ASC;

title: Preserve Unassigned Staff via LEFT JOIN
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `employees` to `assignments` on `emp_id`. Return `e.emp_id`, `e.first_name`, and `a.project_id`. Order results by `e.emp_id` ascending, then `a.project_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN employees to assignments
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, a.project_id
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN assignments a ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, a.project_id FROM employees e LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC, a.project_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Employees without current project assignments appear in the output with a NULL project_id.
common_mistakes: Using an INNER JOIN which drops bench/unassigned employees.
interview_tip: In resource allocation dashboards, outer joins ensure unallocated capacity is visible.
hints: Query: SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, a.project_id FROM employees e LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC, a.project_id ASC;

title: Display Complete Student Body with Optional Course IDs
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `students` to `enrollments` on `student_id`. Return `s.student_id`, `s.first_name`, and `e.course_id`. Order by `s.student_id` ascending, then `e.course_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN students to enrollments
SELECT s.student_id, s.first_name, e.course_id
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s.student_id, s.first_name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id ORDER BY s.student_id ASC, e.course_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Guarantees new or non-enrolled students are retained in institutional reporting.
common_mistakes: Filtering on e.course_id IS NOT NULL in WHERE, inadvertently turning it into an INNER JOIN.
interview_tip: Never place WHERE conditions on the right table in a LEFT JOIN unless you are writing an anti-join.
hints: Query: SELECT s.student_id, s.first_name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id ORDER BY s.student_id ASC, e.course_id ASC;

title: Inspect Product Catalog with Optional Sales Activity
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `products` to `order_items` on `product_id`. Return `p.product_id`, `p.product_name`, and `oi.quantity`. Order by `p.product_id` ascending, then `oi.order_item_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN products to order_items
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id ORDER BY p.product_id ASC, oi.order_item_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Shows all catalog items, retaining unsold inventory with NULL quantity values.
common_mistakes: Joining order_items to products as a LEFT JOIN instead of starting from products.
interview_tip: The table that must preserve all rows goes on the left side of a LEFT JOIN.
hints: Query: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id ORDER BY p.product_id ASC, oi.order_item_id ASC;

title: Display Departments with Associated Projects

LEFT JOIN projects p ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_id ASC, p.project_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Includes departments like Legal and HR that may not currently have any active development projects.

interview_tip: Sorting by primary keys guarantees stable ordering across database engines.

title: Catalog All Courses with Optional Instructor Names
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `courses` to `professors` on `professor_id`. Return `c.course_code`, `c.course_name`, and `p.last_name`. Order by `c.course_code` ascending, then `p.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN courses to professors
SELECT c.course_code, c.course_name, p.last_name
FROM courses c
LEFT JOIN professors p ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.course_code, c.course_name, p.last_name FROM courses c LEFT JOIN professors p ON c.professor_id = p.professor_id ORDER BY c.course_code ASC, p.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Retains courses that have not yet had a primary professor assigned (e.g. independent research courses).
common_mistakes: Using RIGHT JOIN without swapping the table order.
interview_tip: LEFT JOIN is universally preferred over RIGHT JOIN for cognitive readability.
hints: Query: SELECT c.course_code, c.course_name, p.last_name FROM courses c LEFT JOIN professors p ON c.professor_id = p.professor_id ORDER BY c.course_code ASC, p.last_name ASC;

title: Preserve All Departments Using RIGHT JOIN
description_markdown: Perform a `RIGHT JOIN` from `projects` to `departments` on `p.dept_id = d.dept_id`. Return `d.dept_name` and `p.project_name`. Order by `d.dept_name` ascending, then `p.project_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- RIGHT JOIN projects to departments
SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name
FROM projects p
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM projects p RIGHT JOIN departments d ON p.dept_id = d.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: A RIGHT JOIN preserves every department from the right table `departments`, even if no projects match on `p.dept_id`.
common_mistakes: Confusing the preserved side of the join.
interview_tip: RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from the table following the RIGHT JOIN keyword.
hints: Syntax: `FROM projects p RIGHT JOIN departments d ON p.dept_id = d.dept_id`.
Query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM projects p RIGHT JOIN departments d ON p.dept_id = d.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;

title: List Categories with Optional Catalog Products

SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name

solution_query: SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name FROM categories c LEFT JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Displays categories regardless of whether products have been uploaded to them yet.
common_mistakes: Filtering products in WHERE, which discards empty categories.
interview_tip: Any category structure needs outer joins to report on unpopulated taxonomic nodes.
hints: Query: SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name FROM categories c LEFT JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, p.product_name ASC;

title: List All Faculty with Optional Course Assignments
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `professors` to `courses` on `professor_id`. Return `p.professor_id`, `p.last_name`, and `c.course_code`. Order by `p.professor_id` ascending, then `c.course_code` ascending.

SELECT p.professor_id, p.last_name, c.course_code

solution_query: SELECT p.professor_id, p.last_name, c.course_code FROM professors p LEFT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id ORDER BY p.professor_id ASC, c.course_code ASC;

hints: Query: SELECT p.professor_id, p.last_name, c.course_code FROM professors p LEFT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id ORDER BY p.professor_id ASC, c.course_code ASC;

title: Inspect Order Transactions with Payment Status
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `orders` to `payments` on `order_id`. Return `o.order_id`, `o.total_amount`, and `pay.payment_status`. Order by `o.order_id` ascending, then `pay.payment_id` ascending.

-- LEFT JOIN orders and payments
SELECT o.order_id, o.total_amount, pay.payment_status
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments pay ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT o.order_id, o.total_amount, pay.payment_status FROM orders o LEFT JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, pay.payment_id ASC;

title: Default Missing Order Status via COALESCE
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`. Return `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, and `COALESCE(o.order_status, 'No Orders') AS status_label`. Order results by `c.customer_id` ascending, then `status_label` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN with COALESCE fallback label
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE(o.order_status, 'No Orders') AS status_label
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE(o.order_status, 'No Orders') AS status_label FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC, status_label ASC;
solution_explanation: Replaces missing outer-joined order statuses with an informative string constant using standard ANSI COALESCE.
common_mistakes: Using IFNULL which is MySQL-specific and violates cross-dialect ANSI standards.
interview_tip: COALESCE is standard ANSI SQL and supported universally across PostgreSQL and MySQL.
hints: Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE(o.order_status, 'No Orders') AS status_label FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC, status_label ASC;

title: Count Active Projects per Department (Including Zero)
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `departments` to `projects` on `dept_id`. Group by `d.dept_id` and `d.dept_name`. Return `d.dept_name` and `COUNT(p.project_id) AS project_count`. Order by `project_count` descending, then `d.dept_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- LEFT JOIN and aggregate project count
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(p.project_id) AS project_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN projects p ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(p.project_id) AS project_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY project_count DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_explanation: COUNT(p.project_id) evaluates to 0 when project_id is NULL, correctly recording departments without projects.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(*) which incorrectly returns 1 for departments with no projects.
interview_tip: Never use COUNT(*) after an outer join; always count a primary key column from the nullable table.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(p.project_id) AS project_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY project_count DESC, d.dept_name ASC;

title: Count Orders per Customer Including Inactive Accounts
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`. Group by `c.customer_id` and `c.first_name`. Return `c.first_name` and `COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count`. Order by `order_count` descending, then `c.first_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Count orders per customer including zero
SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY order_count DESC, c.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Counts orders per customer while preserving customers with 0 orders via COUNT(o.order_id).
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(*) which turns 0 into 1 for customers without orders.
interview_tip: This is one of the classic SQL interview traps: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) on outer joins.
hints: Query: SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY order_count DESC, c.first_name ASC;

title: Tally Student Course Enrollments with Non-Enrolled Preserved
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `students` to `enrollments` on `student_id`. Group by `s.student_id` and `s.first_name`. Return `s.first_name` and `COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS enrollment_count`. Order by `enrollment_count` descending, then `s.first_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Count enrollments per student
SELECT s.first_name, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS enrollment_count
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s.first_name, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS enrollment_count FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name ORDER BY enrollment_count DESC, s.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Counts enrollments per student while accurately reporting 0 for freshmen or undeclared students who have not enrolled yet.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(e.enrollment_id).
interview_tip: When evaluating course load distributions, outer joins prevent enrollment-blind bias.
hints: Query: SELECT s.first_name, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS enrollment_count FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name ORDER BY enrollment_count DESC, s.first_name ASC;

title: Sum Work Hours per Employee with Default Zero
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `employees` to `assignments` on `emp_id`. Group by `e.emp_id`, `e.first_name`, and `e.last_name`. Return `e.first_name`, `e.last_name`, and `COALESCE(SUM(a.hours_worked), 0) AS total_hours`. Order by `total_hours` descending, then `e.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Sum hours per employee with COALESCE
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, COALESCE(SUM(a.hours_worked), 0) AS total_hours
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN assignments a ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, COALESCE(SUM(a.hours_worked), 0) AS total_hours FROM employees e LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.last_name ORDER BY total_hours DESC, e.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: SUM(a.hours_worked) yields NULL for unassigned staff; COALESCE converts those NULLs into clean 0 values.
common_mistakes: Leaving SUM(a.hours_worked) uncoalesced, resulting in NULLs.
interview_tip: Always coalesce numeric aggregates from outer joins when representing totals or balances.
hints: Query: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, COALESCE(SUM(a.hours_worked), 0) AS total_hours FROM employees e LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.last_name ORDER BY total_hours DESC, e.last_name ASC;

title: Calculate Total Units Sold per Product Including Zero
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `products` to `order_items` on `product_id`. Group by `p.product_id` and `p.product_name`. Return `p.product_name` and `COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS units_sold`. Order by `units_sold` descending, then `p.product_name` ascending.
starter_query:

SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS units_sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS units_sold FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name ORDER BY units_sold DESC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Aggregates total sold volume while preserving unpurchased inventory with 0 units sold.
common_mistakes: Using INNER JOIN which hides items that have never sold.
interview_tip: Inventory analysis requires knowing what doesn't sell just as much as knowing what does.
hints: Query: SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS units_sold FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name ORDER BY units_sold DESC, p.product_name ASC;

title: Calculate Complete Department Headcounts
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `departments` to `employees` on `dept_id`. Group by `d.dept_id` and `d.dept_name`. Return `d.dept_name` and `COUNT(e.emp_id) AS total_employees`. Order by `total_employees` descending, then `d.dept_name` ascending.

solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS total_employees FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY total_employees DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Includes empty departments with 0 headcounts by counting the non-null employee ID.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(*) which would report 1 for an empty department.
interview_tip: COUNT(column) evaluates to 0 on NULLs, which makes it safe for outer join counting.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS total_employees FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY total_employees DESC, d.dept_name ASC;

title: Count Courses Taught per Professor Including Sabbatical
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `professors` to `courses` on `professor_id`. Group by `p.professor_id` and `p.last_name`. Return `p.last_name` and `COUNT(c.course_id) AS course_count`. Order by `course_count` descending, then `p.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join professors to courses and count
SELECT p.last_name, COUNT(c.course_id) AS course_count

solution_query: SELECT p.last_name, COUNT(c.course_id) AS course_count FROM professors p LEFT JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id GROUP BY p.professor_id, p.last_name ORDER BY course_count DESC, p.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Counts assigned courses per professor while including non-teaching faculty with a count of 0.

interview_tip: Group by the primary key p.professor_id along with display columns.

title: Count Products per Category Including Empty Categories
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `categories` to `products` on `category_id`. Group by `c.category_id` and `c.category_name`. Return `c.category_name` and `COUNT(p.product_id) AS product_count`. Order by `product_count` descending, then `c.category_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join categories and products
SELECT c.category_name, COUNT(p.product_id) AS product_count
FROM categories c
LEFT JOIN products p ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.category_name, COUNT(p.product_id) AS product_count FROM categories c LEFT JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id GROUP BY c.category_id, c.category_name ORDER BY product_count DESC, c.category_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Counts active merchandise per category, presenting 0 for unused or empty categories.
common_mistakes: Counting category_id instead of p.product_id.
interview_tip: To count child records in an outer join, always pass the child primary key to COUNT.
hints: Query: SELECT c.category_name, COUNT(p.product_id) AS product_count FROM categories c LEFT JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id GROUP BY c.category_id, c.category_name ORDER BY product_count DESC, c.category_name ASC;

title: Calculate Lifetime Customer Spend with Predicate in ON Clause
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `customers` to `orders` on `c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed'`. Group by `c.customer_id` and `c.first_name`. Return `c.first_name` and `COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent`. Order by `total_spent` descending, then `c.first_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join with predicate in ON clause
SELECT c.first_name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed'
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Placing `o.order_status = 'completed'` in the ON clause preserves customers with only cancelled/refunded orders (or no orders), correctly listing them with 0 total spend.
common_mistakes: Placing the order_status filter in the WHERE clause, which turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
interview_tip: This is a quintessential senior SQL interview pattern: filtering a right table in the ON clause vs the WHERE clause.
hints: Keep `AND o.order_status = 'completed'` inside the `ON` clause, NOT in `WHERE`.

Query: SELECT c.first_name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) AS total_spent FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.first_name ASC;

starter_query:
-- Left join departments to employees and sum salary
SELECT d.dept_name, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS total_salary
FROM departments d

GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS total_salary FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY total_salary DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Calculates total compensation expenditure per department, returning 0 for departments with zero personnel.
common_mistakes: Leaving empty departments without a 0 default.
interview_tip: Executive reporting requires complete departmental representation, even for unstaffed corporate entities.

title: Inspect Product Catalog with Optional Customer Reviews
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `products` to `reviews` on `product_id`. Return `p.product_id`, `p.product_name`, and `r.rating`. Order by `p.product_id` ascending, then `r.review_id` ascending.

SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, r.rating
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, r.rating FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id ORDER BY p.product_id ASC, r.review_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Surfaces all products alongside customer ratings, identifying items that have received no feedback yet.
common_mistakes: Using INNER JOIN which conceals unreviewed products.
interview_tip: Unreviewed inventory is a major merchandising focus in e-commerce merchandising pipelines.

title: Calculate Product Average Rating Defaulting to Zero
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `products` to `reviews` on `product_id`. Group by `p.product_id` and `p.product_name`. Return `p.product_name` and `COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2), 0) AS avg_rating`. Order by `avg_rating` descending, then `p.product_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Calculate average review rating with 0 fallback
SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2), 0) AS avg_rating
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2), 0) AS avg_rating FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name ORDER BY avg_rating DESC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Computes average star ratings for products, substituting 0 for products with zero customer reviews.
common_mistakes: Applying COALESCE inside AVG rather than wrapping AVG.
interview_tip: COALESCE around the entire aggregate ensures that an empty set (which yields NULL) is transformed to 0.
hints: Query: SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2), 0) AS avg_rating FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name ORDER BY avg_rating DESC, p.product_name ASC;

Return `e.student_id`, `e.course_id`, and `COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2), 0) AS avg_mark`. Order by `e.student_id` ascending, then `e.course_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join enrollments to marks
SELECT e.student_id, e.course_id, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2), 0) AS avg_mark
FROM enrollments e
LEFT JOIN marks m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.student_id, e.course_id, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2), 0) AS avg_mark FROM enrollments e LEFT JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id GROUP BY e.enrollment_id, e.student_id, e.course_id ORDER BY e.student_id ASC, e.course_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Retains newly enrolled students who have not yet taken any exams, displaying 0 as their mark average.
common_mistakes: Omitting enrollment_id from the GROUP BY clause.
interview_tip: Outer joins are critical in grading portals where courses currently in progress have no graded items yet.

title: Filter Outer Join on High Hours in the ON Clause
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `employees` to `assignments` on `e.emp_id = a.emp_id AND a.hours_worked > 400`. Return `e.emp_id`, `e.first_name`, `a.project_id`, and `a.hours_worked`. Order by `e.emp_id` ascending, then `a.project_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join with condition in ON clause
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, a.project_id, a.hours_worked
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id AND a.hours_worked > 400
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, a.project_id, a.hours_worked FROM employees e LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id AND a.hours_worked > 400 ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC, a.project_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Because the filter `a.hours_worked > 400` is in the ON clause, all employees remain in the result set, showing NULL project values if they have not logged > 400 hours.
common_mistakes: Putting the filter in WHERE, which strips out employees with <= 400 hours.
interview_tip: In SQL, predicates in the ON clause filter the right table before the join, while WHERE filters after the join.
hints: Query: SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, a.project_id, a.hours_worked FROM employees e LEFT JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id AND a.hours_worked > 400 ORDER BY e.emp_id ASC, a.project_id ASC;

title: Reconcile Departments and Projects via Full Outer Join
description_markdown: Reconcile `departments` and `projects` on `dept_id` using a FULL OUTER JOIN (emulated via UNION in MySQL). Return `COALESCE(d.dept_name, 'No Dept') AS dept_name` and `COALESCE(p.project_name, 'No Project') AS project_name`. Order by `dept_name` ascending, then `project_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Emulate FULL OUTER JOIN via UNION in MySQL
SELECT COALESCE(d.dept_name, 'No Dept') AS dept_name, COALESCE(p.project_name, 'No Project') AS project_name
FROM departments d LEFT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id
UNION
SELECT COALESCE(d.dept_name, 'No Dept') AS dept_name, COALESCE(p.project_name, 'No Project') AS project_name
FROM departments d RIGHT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id
ORDER BY dept_name ASC, project_name ASC;
solution_query: SELECT COALESCE(d.dept_name, 'No Dept') AS dept_name, COALESCE(p.project_name, 'No Project') AS project_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id UNION SELECT COALESCE(d.dept_name, 'No Dept') AS dept_name, COALESCE(p.project_name, 'No Project') AS project_name FROM departments d RIGHT JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id ORDER BY dept_name ASC, project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: PostgreSQL natively supports FULL OUTER JOIN. In MySQL, FULL OUTER JOIN is emulated by combining a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION.
common_mistakes: Using FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL, which produces a syntax error.
interview_tip: MySQL lacks native FULL OUTER JOIN support. Knowing how to emulate it with UNION is a critical interview test.
dialect_notes: PostgreSQL supports native FULL OUTER JOIN. MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN syntax; emulate it by combining LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN using UNION.
hints: In PostgreSQL, use `FROM departments d FULL OUTER JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id`.
In MySQL, combine `LEFT JOIN` and `RIGHT JOIN` queries using `UNION`.

PostgreSQL Query: SELECT COALESCE(d.dept_name, 'No Dept') AS dept_name, COALESCE(p.project_name, 'No Project') AS project_name FROM departments d FULL OUTER JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id ORDER BY dept_name ASC, project_name ASC;

title: Complete Reconciliation of Products and Reviews
description_markdown: Reconcile `products` and `reviews` on `product_id` using a FULL OUTER JOIN (emulated via UNION in MySQL). Return `COALESCE(p.product_name, 'Uncatalogued Product') AS product_name` and `COALESCE(r.rating, 0) AS review_rating`. Order by `product_name` ascending, then `review_rating` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Emulate FULL OUTER JOIN via UNION in MySQL
SELECT COALESCE(p.product_name, 'Uncatalogued Product') AS product_name, COALESCE(r.rating, 0) AS review_rating
FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id
UNION
SELECT COALESCE(p.product_name, 'Uncatalogued Product') AS product_name, COALESCE(r.rating, 0) AS review_rating
FROM products p RIGHT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id
ORDER BY product_name ASC, review_rating ASC;
solution_query: SELECT COALESCE(p.product_name, 'Uncatalogued Product') AS product_name, COALESCE(r.rating, 0) AS review_rating FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id UNION SELECT COALESCE(p.product_name, 'Uncatalogued Product') AS product_name, COALESCE(r.rating, 0) AS review_rating FROM products p RIGHT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id ORDER BY product_name ASC, review_rating ASC;
solution_explanation: Ensures catalog products without reviews and any orphaned reviews are both retained.
common_mistakes: Using UNION ALL instead of UNION, which would duplicate matching rows.
interview_tip: UNION de-duplicates the overlapping inner join rows produced by LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN.
dialect_notes: PostgreSQL implements native FULL OUTER JOIN syntax. In MySQL, combine LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN queries with UNION to eliminate duplicates.
hints: In MySQL: `LEFT JOIN ... UNION ... RIGHT JOIN`.

PostgreSQL Query: SELECT COALESCE(p.product_name, 'Uncatalogued Product') AS product_name, COALESCE(r.rating, 0) AS review_rating FROM products p FULL OUTER JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id ORDER BY product_name ASC, review_rating ASC;

title: Detect Customers with Zero Orders via Outer Join and HAVING
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`. Group by `c.customer_id` and `c.first_name`. Filter using `HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) = 0`. Return `c.customer_id` and `c.first_name`. Order by `c.customer_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join and HAVING count = 0
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) = 0 ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Grouping after a LEFT JOIN and filtering with HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) = 0 identifies customers who have placed exactly zero orders.
common_mistakes: Using HAVING COUNT(*) = 0, which never evaluates to true because the left table row always exists.
interview_tip: COUNT(*) counts rows in the grouped result (at least 1 for the left row), whereas COUNT(o.order_id) counts non-null order IDs (0 when unmatched).
hints: Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) = 0 ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;

title: Detect Unstaffed Departments via Outer Join and HAVING
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `departments` to `employees` on `dept_id`. Group by `d.dept_id` and `d.dept_name`. Filter using `HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) = 0`. Return `d.dept_id` and `d.dept_name`. Order by `d.dept_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Left join and HAVING count = 0
SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) = 0 ORDER BY d.dept_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Identifies organizational departments with 0 assigned staff by checking HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) = 0 on an outer join.
common_mistakes: Using INNER JOIN or COUNT(*).
interview_tip: This is the group-by alternative to an anti-join, frequently used when reporting on aggregates alongside exclusions.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) = 0 ORDER BY d.dept_id ASC;
